iut_type: Bluetooth module (Hosiden wristband/smartwatch device) combining an existing Controller Subsystem QDID and Host Subsystem QDID -- post-2024 inter-layer ICS consistency check cascade and the SoC-as-Core-Controller-with-RF-PHY-report alternative strategy
customer_question: We want to register our module by combining an existing SoC's Controller Subsystem QDID with a Host Subsystem QDID, and we'd like the registration to receive a Design Number (DN) so our downstream set-maker customers can cleanly Include it in their own product registrations. Is this possible with the QDID combination we've specified?
question_variants: If the inter-layer consistency check fails, can we just fix the flagged GAP item to resolve it?
If a DN-bearing registration isn't achievable with this QDID combination, is there an alternative way to still get a marketable DN for our module?
actual_issue: The customer's requested QDID combination (an existing SoC's Controller Subsystem registration plus a Host Subsystem registration) failed the post-2024 registration site's inter-layer ICS consistency check, which is now required to obtain a Design Number (DN) when combining existing QDIDs -- and the consultant's attempt to resolve the specific flagged inconsistency by editing one layer's ICS triggered a cascading expansion of newly-required Mandatory test items rather than a clean fix.
plain_english_explanation: Since the registration site's July 2024 update, combining an existing Controller Subsystem QDID and Host Subsystem QDID offers two distinct paths: (a) a DN-bearing registration, which requires passing an inter-layer ICS consistency check between the two layers, or (b) an old Declaration-registration-equivalent path ('Combine unmodified Designs'), which skips that consistency check entirely but does not assign a DN. For path (a), the consultant ran a trial Consistency Check in his own Workspace and found multiple inter-layer inconsistencies, all relating to Periodic Advertising-related features where the GAP layer excluded certain items because the underlying Link Layer (LL) didn't support corresponding features. Attempting to resolve this by simply toggling the GAP layer's Excluded flag from YES to NO triggered a cascading 'whack-a-mole' effect: each fix exposed a fresh wave of newly-required Mandatory test items, because the new site generates ICS-consistent test requirements for whichever layer's ICS gets edited. To achieve a true fix, the customer would need to either select a different SoC whose LL genuinely supports the relevant features, or select a different Host Stack whose GAP doesn't claim support it can't back up -- but in this case, the existing GAP-layer Host Stack's Listing company had withdrawn its SIG membership, making a corrective re-registration request to update its GAP features impractical. Since changing Host Stack was therefore impractical, the consultant proposed a structurally different alternative: since the SoC in question is technically supposed to be Component-registered (not Controller-Subsystem-registered) and requires RF PHY testing on the actual module/board it's mounted on regardless, the customer's module could Include ONLY the SoC's QDID (not the Host Subsystem), pass Consistency Check cleanly (Invalid=0) on that narrower basis, and obtain its own DN via a Core Controller (formerly Controller Subsystem) registration by uploading the module's own RF PHY test report. The downstream set-maker could then Include both the module's new DN (Core Controller) and the Host Controller's existing QDID via 'Combine unmodified Designs,' completely avoiding the inter-layer inconsistency problem while still achieving a Core Complete product registration. This approach has the added marketing benefit that the module itself becomes 'Design-registered' with its own DN, since the RF PHY test was run and uploaded specifically for the module.
consultant_answer: Your requested QDID combination fails the new site's inter-layer consistency check (several Periodic Advertising-related GAP items are excluded because the underlying SoC's Link Layer doesn't support the corresponding features) -- and trying to fix this by editing the GAP layer cascades into a large new set of Mandatory test requirements, so I stopped before going further down that path. A clean fix would require switching to an SoC or Host Stack that doesn't have this mismatch, but the current Host Stack's Listing company has withdrawn from SIG membership, making a corrective update impractical. I'd recommend an alternative instead: since your SoC technically requires RF PHY testing on the module regardless, register your module Including only the SoC's QDID, upload an RF PHY test report for it, and obtain your own DN via a Core Controller registration. Your downstream set-maker customers can then Include both your module's new DN and the existing Host Controller QDID unmodified, avoiding the inconsistency problem entirely while giving your module its own marketable, Design-registered DN.
decision_logic: When combining an existing Controller Subsystem QDID and Host Subsystem QDID for a DN-bearing registration, first run a trial Consistency Check to detect inter-layer ICS inconsistencies; if editing the flagged layer's ICS to resolve them triggers a cascading expansion of new Mandatory test requirements, check whether changing the SoC or Host Stack to one without the mismatch is realistic (it may not be, e.g., if the Listing company has withdrawn from SIG membership) -- if not realistic, consider restructuring the registration so the SoC alone (with its own RF PHY test report) obtains a DN via Core Controller registration, letting downstream customers Include that DN plus the Host Controller QDID unmodified to sidestep the inconsistency check entirely.
final_recommendation: When a customer's desired existing-QDID combination fails the inter-layer consistency check, don't just attempt a direct ICS edit without warning about the cascading Mandatory-requirement risk -- check the practicality of switching components first, and if that's blocked (e.g., by a withdrawn Listing company), proactively propose the SoC-as-Core-Controller-with-RF-PHY-report restructuring as an alternative that preserves DN-bearing registration value for both the module seller and downstream customers.
risk_if_done_wrong: A customer or consultant naively editing a flagged ICS layer to resolve an inter-layer inconsistency without anticipating the cascading effect could end up committing to a much larger, more expensive test scope than originally planned; conversely, registering via the no-DN Declaration-equivalent path without considering the restructuring alternative could leave the module without a marketable DN, undermining its value for OEM/set-maker customers.
